strengths: Compelling and well-motivated problem formulation: Extending referring video object segmentation (RVOS) to interaction-aware scenarios (InterRVOS) by modeling both actor and target entities addresses a major limitation of prior benchmarks that focus primarily on isolated single objects or collective multi-instance motions.

Comprehensive and well-designed data generation pipeline: The four-stage annotation process using GPT-4o and LLaMA-70B effectively transforms VidOR annotations into structured, multi-perspective interaction descriptions, covering appearance, motion-only, multi-instance, and unidirectional/bidirectional interactions at scale (127K expressions across 8.7K videos).

Strong data efficiency and transferability: Experimental results on MeViS (Table 3) show that models trained on InterRVOS subsets outperform models trained on significantly larger datasets like Ref-SAV, particularly in zero-shot transfer settings, underscoring the quality and richness of the interaction-centric annotations.

Clear baseline and informative ablations: The ReVIOSa baseline adapts MLLM + SAM2 effectively by introducing dedicated actor and target segmentation tokens ([SEG_ACT] and [SEG_TAR]). The ablation experiments in Table 6 clearly demonstrate the value of joint actor-target modeling over independent or single-token baselines.
weaknesses: Lack of human audit and quality verification for the automated dataset: Because InterRVOS-8K is fully automatically generated via GPT-4o and LLaMA-70B on top of VidOR, hallucination, incorrect role assignment (actor vs. target inversion), and temporal misalignment are inevitable. The paper does not provide quantitative human verification metrics (e.g., error rate, role consistency, or description accuracy across a sampled subset).

Limited architectural novelty: ReVIOSa builds closely upon the existing Sa2VA framework (marrying SAM2 with an MLLM decoder). The primary architectural change is expanding from a single `[SEG]` token to two role-specific tokens (`[SEG_ACT]` and `[SEG_TAR]`). While effective, the technical modeling contribution is somewhat incremental.

Ambiguity in task definition and evaluation protocol: The paper occasionally switches between defining InterRVOS as segmenting both actor and target from a *pair* of complementary expressions versus segmenting both simultaneously from a *single* expression (as done in ReVIOSa and Figure 4). Making the distinction between paired referring expressions and dual-token extraction from a single prompt explicit earlier in Section 1 and 3 would improve clarity.

Performance degradation on standard benchmarks: In the appendix (Table A2), ReVIOSa-1B performs worse than the Sa2VA-1B baseline on conventional benchmarks like Ref-DAVIS (63.7 vs. 67.1) and Ref-Youtube-VOS (59.3 vs. 61.8). This trade-off between interaction-specialized modeling and standard single-object RVOS performance is relegated to the supplementary material and deserves discussion in the main manuscript.

strengths: Relevant and well-motivated problem formulation: Extending referring video object segmentation (RVOS) from single/isolated object tracking to interaction-aware actor-target segmentation captures essential relational semantics often missed in prior benchmarks.

Comprehensive dataset construction: The InterRVOS-8K dataset provides 127K referring expressions covering single, multi-instance, and actor-target interactions based on VidOR videos, with clearly documented prompts and stage-wise generation procedures.

Solid empirical transfer: Models trained on InterRVOS-8K show strong data efficiency and zero-shot transfer capabilities across conventional RVOS benchmarks such as MeViS, Ref-YouTube-VOS, and Ref-DAVIS.
weaknesses: Lack of human verification and quality audit: Both training and evaluation splits are generated purely via automated LLM/VLM pipelines (GPT-4o and LLaMA-3.1). Without a rigorous human quality check or error analysis on the evaluation set, it is difficult to assess the rate of hallucinated relations, inaccurate role assignments, or noisy ground-truth masks.

Limited architectural novelty: The ReVIOSa architecture is essentially an adaptation of recent MLLM+SAM2 frameworks (such as Sa2VA), where the technical contribution primarily consists of adding a second segmentation token ([SEG_TAR]) alongside the existing referring token rather than proposing novel relational visual reasoning modules.

Ambiguity in handling multi-target and complex interactions: Although statistics show that over 20% of interactions involve three or more entities (e.g., Actor [1] interacting with Targets [2] and [3]), the paper does not clearly specify how the fixed pair of special tokens ([SEG_ACT] and [SEG_TAR]) handles multiple targets—whether they are merged into a single mask or sequentially generated.

Evaluation split source: The evaluation set is carved out of the VidOR training split rather than a standard validation/test set, which warrants clearer justification and comparison against standard relation detection splits.

strengths: The paper identifies a clear gap in conventional RVOS benchmarks, which predominantly focus on single objects or isolated movements without explicitly modeling relational roles (actor vs. target).

The proposed dataset, InterRVOS-8K, is sizable (127K expressions across 8,738 video clips) and provides multi-level descriptions including appearance, motion, multi-instance, and actor-target relational expressions.

The experimental results demonstrate that training on InterRVOS-8K enables competitive or improved performance and data efficiency on existing RVOS benchmarks such as MeViS, Ref-YouTube-VOS, and Ref-DAVIS in both zero-shot and joint training setups.
The baseline model ReVIOSa provides an intuitive and unified way to handle both single-referent and paired actor-target segmentation within an MLLM + SAM2 framework.
weaknesses: Lack of human verification and quality audit: The entire annotation pipeline relies on automated prompting of GPT-4o and LLaMA-70B over VidOR videos. The paper does not provide a quantitative quality check (e.g., human evaluation on a random sample to measure caption-video alignment, role inversion errors, hallucination rates, or mask precision).

Limited architectural novelty: ReVIOSa directly builds upon the existing Sa2VA / LISA paradigm (MLLM backbone + LoRA + SAM2 decoder), with the primary change being the introduction of two distinct special tokens ([SEG_ACT] and [SEG_TAR]) instead of one. The technical contribution on the model side is fairly incremental.

Unclear evaluation protocol for Actor-Target segmentation: The paper should provide a formal mathematical definition of how the J & F metrics are computed in the Actor-Target setting in Table 5 (e.g., whether the score is an average across both actor and target mask tracks, how Hungarian matching or role-to-mask assignment is strictly evaluated, and whether the model is penalized for swapping roles).

Comparison with recent video-grounding MLLMs is limited: While comparison with Sa2VA is fair, additional recent open-source MLLM-based segmentation methods (e.g., VideoGLAMM, VISA, or ROS-LLaVA) are missing from the empirical benchmarks.

strengths: Well-motivated task formulation: Extending RVOS to explicitly decouple and segment both actor and target objects in an interaction addresses an important limitation in relational and interaction-aware video reasoning.

Comprehensive dataset construction: InterRVOS-127K provides a large-scale benchmark (over 127K expressions) built via a detailed four-stage automated pipeline leveraging SAM 2, GPT-4o, and LLaMA-3.1-70B, with a human-verified validation set ensuring high quality.

Effective and principled model design: Introducing dedicated interaction tokens ([SEG_ACT] and [SEG_TAR]) alongside the Attention Mask Loss (AML) is technically sound. Supervising cross-attention directly between segment tokens and visual tokens provides clear empirical gains.

Thorough empirical analysis: The paper includes extensive evaluations, layer-head selection profiling, ablation studies, and cross-dataset zero-shot transfer evaluations on MeViS, Ref-YouTube-VOS, and Ref-DAVIS.
weaknesses: Baseline comparison fairness on target segmentation: Existing RVOS models (e.g., Referformer, Sa2VA) naturally produce only a single mask and thus have '-' in the InterRVOS-Target evaluation. A more rigorous baseline comparison would evaluate these models when prompted twice (e.g., by synthetically decomposing the expression into separate actor and target queries) to benchmark how much gain comes from joint interaction modeling versus simple multi-turn querying.

Scope of interaction modeling: The formulation is primarily restricted to unidirectional/bidirectional binary or simple multi-object interactions with predefined actor/target roles. Extending beyond this rigid role schema to arbitrary relational graphs or multi-party interactions remains underexplored.

Heuristic layer-head selection for AML: The process of manually identifying which layer and heads have high vision attention (e.g., Layer 22 top-4 heads for 1B, Layer 33 top-4 heads for 4B) requires profiling per architecture and may be sensitive to changes in pre-trained model checkpoints or visual backbones.

strengths: Well-motivated task formulation: Extending RVOS to distinguish and segment both actor and target objects (InterRVOS) addresses an important limitation in traditional RVOS benchmarks, where asymmetric inter-object dynamics are often collapsed or ignored.

Substantial dataset contribution: InterRVOS-127K offers a large-scale resource (over 127K expressions) with multi-instance and actor-target annotations, supported by a clear stage-wise generation pipeline and human-verified evaluation set.

Effective and well-analyzed architectural design: ReVIOSa introduces dedicated interaction tokens ([SEG_ACT], [SEG_TAR]) alongside the Attention Mask Loss (AML). The connection between attention concentration and segmentation quality is thoroughly motivated and analyzed across layers and heads.

Comprehensive empirical validation: ReVIOSa achieves strong performance on the proposed benchmark and demonstrates solid data efficiency and zero-shot transfer across standard RVOS benchmarks (MeViS, Ref-Youtube-VOS, Ref-DAVIS).
weaknesses: Baseline comparisons on InterRVOS-Target: Prior methods naturally leave the target column empty in Table 2 because they are single-target RVOS frameworks. A more direct comparison could have included adapted baselines (e.g., querying existing models twice using extracted subject/object referring phrases) to isolate whether gains come from joint modeling or backbone capacity.

Heuristic layer-head selection for AML: The selection of layer and heads for AML supervision relies on empirical searching of attention magnitude to vision tokens, which varies across model sizes (Layer 22 for 1B, Layer 33 for 4B) and may need re-calibration for different architectures.

Lack of inference runtime and efficiency metrics: The framework combines an MLLM (InternVL-2.5) with SAM2; reporting inference latency, frame rate (FPS), and memory footprint would help contextualize its deployment practicality against lightweight RVOS methods.

strengths: Meaningful task formulation: Extending referring video object segmentation (RVOS) to explicitly disambiguate and segment both actor and target roles addresses a key limitation in standard RVOS, where asymmetric interactions are either collapsed or target objects are ignored.

Comprehensive dataset contribution: InterRVOS-127K is a large-scale dataset (over 127K expressions across 8.7K video clips) featuring rich interaction annotations, supported by a clearly structured multi-stage auto-annotation pipeline using GPT-4o and LLaMA-70B with human refinement for the validation set.

Well-motivated architectural design: Introducing role-specific tokens ([SEG_ACT] and [SEG_TAR]) alongside the Attention Mask Loss (AML) provides a targeted mechanism to steer MLLM self-attention toward visual referents, supported by thorough attention analyses across layers and heads (Figures 6, 7, A1, A2).

Solid empirical evaluation: The proposed method demonstrates strong performance on the InterRVOS benchmark as well as solid zero-shot and fine-tuned transferability to standard RVOS benchmarks (MeViS, Ref-YouTube-VOS, Ref-DAVIS), outperforming strong recent baselines such as Sa2VA.
weaknesses: Baseline comparison on InterRVOS-Target: In Table 2, existing RVOS baselines have empty scores on the Target split because they only output a single mask. A fairer comparison could be achieved by prompting existing baselines twice with decomposed language prompts (e.g., querying the actor and target separately) to isolate the benefit of the unified architecture versus task definition.

Handling of multi-entity interactions (>2 objects): Dataset statistics indicate that 20.3% of interactions involve three or more objects (Figure A8(h)), yet the framework primarily focuses on binary actor-target tokens ([SEG_ACT] and [SEG_TAR]). The manuscript lacks clarity on how the model handles or evaluates scenes with multiple targets or higher-order interactions.

Generalization and automation of layer-head selection: The selection protocol for AML relies on empirical inspection of attention magnitude per model scale (e.g., Layer 22 for 1B, Layer 33 for 4B). A discussion or validation on whether this head-selection criterion generalizes across different model families (e.g., Qwen-VL or older LLaVA backbones) without extensive manual tuning would strengthen the contribution.

Quality assessment of automated pseudo-labels: While the evaluation set was human-verified, the vast majority of the 122K training expressions and tracks rely on automated GPT-4o and SAM2 extraction. A quantitative quality check or error analysis on a representative training sample (e.g., percentage of tracking drift or caption hallucination) is missing.
